lead: Linux stores everything in one tree. The tree hangs from a single directory, /, called the root directory. Directories, ordinary files, devices and sockets all sit in that tree. There is no C: drive. One set of commands, one set of permissions and one way of naming things then work everywhere. When you run ls in your home directory, install a package, or read a log in /var/log after a service fails, you walk the same tree. This chapter maps the tree, explains paths, and names the seven file types that every directory entry belongs to.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, the kernel and user space split, and the basic command line (pwd, cd, ls).

blocks.text: Every mounted disk joins the same tree. A USB stick does not become a new drive letter; it appears as a directory such as /media/ravi/stick. The top level is fixed by convention so that scripts and users find the same things on every machine.

items: /bin: user commands such as ls and cp.
/sbin: system administration commands, used at boot and by root.
/boot: the kernel image and boot loader files.
/dev: device files, one per disk, terminal and so on.
/etc: configuration files, almost always plain text.
/home: one directory per user, such as /home/ravi.
/lib: shared libraries and kernel modules.
/media and /mnt: mount points for removable disks and for temporary mounts.
/opt: add-on software installed outside the normal command packages.
/proc: kernel and process information, generated on demand.
/root: the home directory of the root user, not the root directory.
/srv: data served by this machine, such as web pages.
/tmp: temporary files; any user may write here.
/usr: programs, libraries and documentation; /usr/bin holds most commands on modern systems.
/var: files that change size, such as logs in /var/log, print spool and package caches.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this layout the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). Fixing the names matters: a shell script written on one machine still finds /etc/passwd and /var/log on the next.

sections.h3: Paths: absolute, relative, and how the kernel walks one

blocks.text: An absolute path starts at / and is complete, like /home/ravi/notes.txt. A relative path starts at the current working directory, which pwd prints. If you stand in /home/ravi, then notes.txt, lab/notes.txt and ../ravi are all relative paths.

items: Start at / for an absolute path, or at the process's current directory for a relative one.
Split the path at each / character into components.
Look up the next component by name inside the current directory. This lookup needs execute (x) permission on that directory.
A component of . means the directory itself; .. means its parent directory.
If the component is a symbolic link, replace it with the link's target and continue. A counter stops after too many links, which kills loops.
Open the final component. The kernel returns that file's inode number, and the path name is no longer used.

blocks.text: The kernel caps one path name passed to a system call at PATH_MAX, 4096 bytes including the terminating null byte, so about 4095 usable bytes. Deeper nesting is fine as long as the path string stays under the cap.
Every entry is one of seven types. The first character of an ls -l line gives the type; the next nine characters are permissions (see 2.4).

blocks.text: A directory entry maps a name to an inode number. The inode stores the type, owner, permissions, size, timestamps and the addresses of the data blocks; the name is not inside the inode. That is why two names can share one file, and the link count becomes 2 (see 2.3).

/proc and /sys are virtual file systems. They use no disk blocks. /proc/1234 describes the process with PID 1234, /proc/meminfo reports memory, and /sys/class/net lists network devices. Reading such a file runs kernel code and builds the text at that moment.

spec.title: The listing entries under /home/ravi
spec.aria: A tree from the root directory through home and ravi to the four listing entries: notes.txt a regular file of 2148 bytes and 1 link, lab a directory with 2 links, latest a symlink of 9 bytes pointing to notes.txt, and tty1 a character device with major 4 and minor 1.

examples.question:
A listing of /home/ravi shows four lines:
-rw-r--r-- 1 ravi students 2148 Jan  5 10:20 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x 2 ravi students 4096 Jan  5 09:00 lab
lrwxrwxrwx 1 ravi students    9 Jan  4 18:02 latest -> notes.txt
crw--w---- 1 root tty      4,   1 Jan  5 08:00 tty1
(a) Give the file type of each line. (b) Explain why the link counts are 1, 2, 1 and 1. (c) Say what 2148 counts. (d) Standing in /home/ravi/lab, give the absolute path reached by ../latest and the type of the final file after the link is followed.
steps: Line 1 begins with -, so notes.txt is a regular file. Line 2 begins with d, so lab is a directory. Line 3 begins with l, so latest is a symbolic link. Line 4 begins with c, so tty1 is a character device.
notes.txt has one name, so its link count is 1.
lab shows link count 2, so it has no subdirectories: the two links are the . entry inside lab and the name lab in /home/ravi. Each subdirectory would add one more.
latest is a symbolic link with one name, so its link count is 1.
tty1 has one name, so its link count is 1.
2148 is the size of notes.txt in bytes, that is 2148 bytes.
The 9 on the link line is the length in bytes of the target string notes.txt, which has 9 characters.
On the device line, 4 and 1 are the major and minor numbers, not a byte count. Major 4 selects the terminal driver; minor 1 selects one terminal.

Start at /home/ravi/lab. The component .. moves to /home/ravi. Then latest is a symbolic link whose target is notes.txt; resolved against the link's own directory /home/ravi, it becomes /home/ravi/notes.txt.
The final file /home/ravi/notes.txt has three name components, home, ravi and notes.txt. It is the regular file from line 1.
examples.answer: Types: regular, directory, symbolic link, character device. Link counts: 1, 2, 1, 1. Size 2148 bytes. The path is /home/ravi/notes.txt, the regular file from line 1, with three components.

traps: The first character of an ls -l line is the file type, not a permission. A leading d or l does not mean 'no permission'.
On a device line the pair 4, 1 is major,minor. Students often read it as a size or as a date.
/root is the home directory of the root user. The root directory is / alone.
A symbolic link's size is the length of its target string, not the size of the target file, and its link count is 1.
/proc files often show size 0 yet return text when read, because they are generated on demand.

quiz.q: Name five top-level directories and one thing each holds.
quiz.a: Any five: /bin commands, /etc configuration, /home user files, /var logs, /dev device files, /proc kernel information.

quiz.q: Why does a directory with no subdirectories show link count 2?
quiz.a: One link is the . entry inside it; the other is its own name in the parent directory. Each subdirectory would add one more.

quiz.q: Standing in /home/ravi/lab, give the absolute path reached by ../../../etc/passwd.
quiz.a: .. gives /home/ravi, then /home, then /. So the path is /etc/passwd.

quiz.q: An ls -l line reads brw-rw---- 1 root disk 8, 0 Jan 5 08:00 sda. State the file type, the link count, and what 8 and 0 mean.
quiz.a: Block device; link count 1; 8 is the major number selecting the driver and 0 is the minor number selecting the disk.

quiz.q: A file in /proc shows size 0 but prints several lines when read. Explain.
quiz.a: /proc is a virtual file system with no disk blocks. The kernel builds the text when read is called, so the stored size is 0 and does not reflect the output length.

quiz.q: A line reads lrwxrwxrwx 1 ravi students 13 Jan 4 18:02 conf -> /etc/app.conf. What does 13 count, and what happens on opening conf after /etc/app.conf is deleted?
quiz.a: 13 is the length in bytes of the target string /etc/app.conf. After deletion the link still exists, but opening it fails with 'No such file or directory' because the target is gone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Containers reuse this tree: an image is a stack of read-only layers joined under /, and overlayfs makes them look like one directory. /proc and /sys are how ordinary tools read kernel state: top, ps and free read /proc, while udev reads /sys/class and /sys/devices to create device files. Newer work pushes the same idea further with user-space file systems, where a program answers the lookups. Search for overlayfs, sysfs, FUSE and mount namespaces to go deeper.
